title: SPE Chapter 09 — Blog

scenes.narr: Chapter nine is the finale: a complete content system — a blog, static pages, and the tutorial's own documentation — all built on the foundation of the last eight chapters.
The trick that keeps it small is a single enum. Post, or Doc — that one value is the only thing that distinguishes the two kinds of content.
Because one shared, abstract engine does all the work. It opens reading to everyone and restricts writing to admins, once, for every content type.
Its list method filters by type, optionally by tag, and paginates — one implementation serving both the blog and the docs.
So the entire Blog plugin is this: extend the engine, and declare that its type is Post.
And Docs is the same engine again, declaring only that its type is Doc. Two features, almost no extra code.
Here are the docs — the very same list engine, showing a different kind of content.
A post's rendered HTML and its excerpt are property hooks — computed from the stored Markdown the moment they are read, so they can never go stale.
And the Markdown renderer is safe by construction: it escapes the input first, before parsing, so no raw HTML can ever slip through.
This post was written in Markdown and rendered to safe HTML — headings, emphasis, and links, with nothing dangerous allowed.
Links are checked against an allow-list of schemes using PHP's new URI parser: http, https, and mailto pass; a javascript link is rejected outright.
Underneath, one posts table carries the type column, and a pair of tag tables give proper many-to-many tagging.
Saving a post rebuilds its tags, de-duplicated by slug, so the same tag written two different ways never doubles up.
And a tag becomes a filter: the same list, narrowed to one subject with a join across those tables.
The navigation adapts to who is looking: everyone sees Home, Blog, and Docs; admins also get Tags and Users.
And that is the Simple PHP Engine: nine short chapters, from a single statement to a complete content system — and never once reaching for a framework.
